body: The phone in his hand holds two years of saved episodes, and at ten past seven in the morning a twenty-six-year-old is going down the list in a van outside a job that does not start for another twenty minutes. There is an interview he has been meaning to get to since March, a series on discipline he downloaded in one enthusiastic evening, and a long conversation that everybody he knows has already quoted at him. He scrolls past all of it twice. Then he puts the phone in the door pocket and sits in the quiet with the engine off until it is time to go in.

He was not short of material. He was short of a decision, at ten past seven, about what kind of hour he wanted, and he could not make one, so he made none. That is not laziness on his part. That is a property of the format.

Podcasts are the dominant format for men under forty, and they are very good at what they do. They are long, they are conversational, and they actually get finished, which is more than most media manages. What they are structurally poor at is regularity.

It is worth being precise about why, because the fault is not in the shows. A habit is a behaviour that has stopped costing a decision. That is the entire definition, and it is why habits survive bad weeks — there is nothing to weigh, so there is nothing to lose the argument with. A podcast can never quite become one, because every listen begins with a choice: which one, which episode, is this the mood for, do I want to be talked at for an hour right now. The choice is small. It is also made several times a week for years on end, and anything that has to be chosen that often is eventually going to be chosen against.

The alternative is not another show. It is a band. The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70, carries 121 stations, and no two of them share a number. Every one is playing at this moment, without reference to whether anybody has opened anything.

Running a station that way costs a great deal more than running a show. A show can be made when there is something to say. A station has to be full at four in the afternoon on a Wednesday in a week when nothing whatever is happening, and it has to be as full then as it is on a good day. That is unglamorous and it is the part that does the work, because the flat Wednesday is the day a habit is kept or lost. A podcast asks you to choose it every time. Anything that has to be chosen every time eventually will not be.

The second problem is harder to say without sounding ungrateful, so here it is plainly: the format optimises for interest. A podcast that is not compelling does not get finished, and so everything in it drifts toward the novel, the contested and the strongly stated. That is a fine diet in moderation and a poor one as a staple. A young man living on it gets extremely well informed about the arguments of the faith and stays oddly unpractised at the thing itself. He can tell you exactly what he believes about worship. He has not sung in a while.

A band is arranged the way a broadcast band is, in blocks — ministry stations together, the nations together in their own languages, the always-on formats together — and the point of the arrangement is that you stop having to look. Learn roughly where a block sits and your hand goes there without your attention. That is a skill a dial teaches and a search box actively prevents, because a search box requires you to name the thing before it will give you anything at all.
Which is the difference in one line. A list waits to be asked. A station is already going.

None of that makes the shows worthless, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. There are men who came back to the faith through a podcast, who learned more doctrine in a year of commutes than in a decade of Sundays, and who would never have opened the book. The format is genuinely good at explaining, at arguing, and at keeping a man company on a long drive. What it cannot do is arrive. It has no way of reaching someone who has not opened it, and the weeks when a man does not open anything are precisely the weeks that decide how the next year goes.
Formation is what happens on the days you were not trying.

There is a joiner in his thirties who keeps a paint-spattered speaker on the shelf above his bench, and it goes on when the lights go on and off when he locks up. He did not choose it as a discipline. It was there when he took the workshop over and he never got round to changing the arrangement. Some mornings he does not notice it for an hour. In March he lost a job he had quoted for and needed, and he stood at that bench most of the morning not doing very much, and the room was not silent while he did it. He would not describe any of that as ministry. He also has not had a silent workshop in six years.
He never had to be in the mood, and he was never asked to be. That is the only reason it was still running on the morning he could not have arranged anything for himself.

The cost is real and there is no point dressing it up. A station will play you things you would not have picked. On a podcast you choose the voice, the subject and the length; on a band you get somebody else’s schedule, and some of it is not for you. There are afternoons on any frequency where you would trade the whole hour for one episode you already know you like.

That is not a defect to be tuned out of the format. It is the format. The reason a station can form a man is precisely that he is not the editor of it, because the man doing the editing only ever edits toward himself. Nobody was ever talked into the song they find themselves humming on a bad afternoon. It was put in front of them repeatedly, by somebody else, at an hour when they were not paying attention, and it stayed.

So the case is not that podcasts are bad and stations are holy. It is narrower than that. One of these builds an appetite and the other builds a habit, and a young man who intends to be different in five years needs the second more than the first. Keep the shows. Listen to them when you have the appetite. But put something underneath them that does not depend on your appetite, because your appetite is going to have an off year at some point, and it will not give you notice.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing in the van. So here is the part that is not theory.

There are 46 frequencies on air, and it is worth knowing what sort of thing is on them before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. Some of it is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. Some of it is family programming, safe enough to leave running in a room with children in it. And 40 of the frequencies are the nations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. Four kinds, one dial, and no menu to work your way through.

If you are twenty-six and sitting in a van, start at HM 315.20 — Corner Cipher. It is the Christian rap frequency, and it is the one to put in front of a young man first, for a reason that follows directly from everything above. Rap is the form most men that age are already fluent in, and it is the one most likely to be listened to rather than tolerated — which matters enormously, because a habit that feels like homework does not survive a month. Corner Cipher is not a lecture with a beat under it. It is a station: bars, worship and testimony running continuously, scheduled hours ago by somebody else, going whether or not you opened anything today. Put it on when the engine starts and leave it alone.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is in the door pocket, press play, and it plays — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band finds out which frequencies young men are actually reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

So do not add it to a list. A list is where good intentions go to be chosen against, and that is the entire argument of this article. Put HM 315.20 on tomorrow morning when you start the van, and then do not decide anything else about it for a fortnight. You will still have the shows. You will simply also have something that was already playing on the morning you had nothing to bring to it, which is the morning that counts.
